readerTitle: On video calls, everyone is fine: leading a team you can't see
caseNote: 가상 사례 (원격 소프트웨어 팀, 세 곳의 게스트하우스를 원격으로 운영하는 사업주) · 적용 레슨으로 심리적 안전감과 역할·책임 개념을 함께 사용
insight: 원격 팀에서는 침묵이 진척처럼 보이므로, 문제를 말하기 쉬운 분위기와 일마다 적힌 담당자를 의도적으로 글로 만들어야 한다.
misconception: 원격 팀의 문제는 감시와 확인을 늘리면 해결된다. 회의와 카메라를 늘리면 무슨 일이 일어나는지 더 잘 보인다.

sources.text: 이 유닛의 개념 레슨 PPL-05-01 (심리적 안전감), PPL-05-03 (역할과 책임)
모든 사례는 설명용 가상 예시이며 통계나 연구 수치를 쓰지 않음

factChecks.note: 모든 사례(원격 소프트웨어 팀, 게스트하우스 세 곳)는 가상입니다. 실제 연구 수치나 기업 사실은 쓰지 않았습니다. 심리적 안전감의 정의 문장이 PPL-05-01 레슨의 정의와 일치하는지 확인하세요.
5번 카드의 네 가지 항목(Owner, Decides, Due, Status)이 PPL-05-03 레슨에서 쓰는 용어와 겹치거나 충돌하지 않는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: On video calls, everyone is "fine."
body: Monday's standup for a remote software team: six faces on a screen, six people saying "on track." On Thursday, the release slips. One developer had been stuck on the same bug since Monday.
Nobody lied, exactly. Working remotely just made silence look like progress.

image.label: Grid of six smiling video-call faces, one hiding a worried note
image.brief: 화상회의 화면 6분할. 다섯 명은 웃으며 엄지를 들고 있고, 한 명도 웃고 있지만 화면 밖 책상 위에 'stuck since Mon'이라고 쓴 포스트잇이 살짝 보임. 따뜻한 플랫 일러스트. 실제 화상회의 앱 로고나 UI는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Why didn't she say anything?
body: You lead this team across three time zones. The stuck developer tells you two things: she didn't want to look slow, and she wasn't sure whose call the fix was.

options.text: Add a second daily check-in and ask everyone to keep cameras on
options.feedback: More watching gets you more updates but less truth. If people already fear looking slow, extra checks make hiding the smarter move.

options.text: Make "blocked" a normal update: share your own stuck points first and thank people who flag early
options.feedback: This targets her first reason, **psychological safety**. When admitting a problem costs nothing, problems surface on Monday, not Thursday.

options.text: Write down one owner for each task and who decides on fixes
options.feedback: This fixes her second reason, unclear **roles**. But a clear owner who still fears looking slow can stay quiet.

cards.title: What a screen hides
body: In a shared room, you notice the sigh, the person staring at the same screen all afternoon, the colleague hovering at someone's desk. Those cues invite help before anyone asks.
Remotely, those cues vanish. Two things this unit covered get harder at once: feeling safe to speak up, and knowing who owns what. Both now have to be built on purpose, mostly in writing.

cards.title: Make bad news cheap to share.
body: **Psychological safety** is the shared belief that you won't be punished for speaking up. Remote teams read it from small signals: how fast a manager answers a problem, and in what tone. Three habits send the right signal:
list: **Go first:** post your own mistakes and open questions in the team channel
**Build it in:** add a "blocked on" line to every written update, so admitting it is routine
**Reply with help:** answer "I'm stuck" with "thanks, what do you need?", never "why so late?"

cards.eyebrow: Concept at work · Roles and accountability
cards.title: One owner, written down.
body: In an office, ownership often lives in hallway talk. Remotely, if it isn't written, it doesn't exist. For each piece of work, one short note answers four questions.

breakdown.label: Decides
breakdown.detail: The owner, or who they should ask

breakdown.label: Due
breakdown.detail: Date plus time zone: "Friday" differs in Lisbon and Seoul

breakdown.label: Status
breakdown.detail: One thread for updates, not five chats

cards.callout: **Roles and accountability** mean someone can always answer "who's on it?"
cards.softwareNote: Many teams put this note right on the ticket or task card, so the owner field is the first thing anyone sees.

cards.title: Now it's three guesthouses.
body: You own three small guesthouses in different towns and run them from your office in the city. Staff share one group chat. A guest's message about a broken heater sat there for two days. Everyone saw it. Nobody fixed it.

image.label: Group chat with a heater complaint and many 'seen' marks
image.brief: 휴대폰 단체 채팅 화면. 'Room 4 heater broken, guest is cold'라는 메시지 아래 '읽음' 표시 눈 아이콘이 여러 개 붙어 있고 답장은 없음. 배경에 작은 게스트하우스 세 채. 실제 메신저 앱 로고나 UI는 쓰지 않음.

options.text: Remind everyone to be more responsive in the chat
options.feedback: It feels like action, but "everyone" is still the owner. When a job belongs to the whole chat, each person assumes someone else has it.

options.text: Name one owner for guest issues at each house, who replies "on it" within an hour
options.feedback: This is **roles and accountability**. The heater now has a person, and the "on it" reply shows everyone it's covered.

options.text: Answer and assign every guest issue yourself
options.feedback: Problems get fixed this week, but you become the bottleneck. Staff learn to wait for you instead of owning the fix.

cards.title: Each fix fails without the other.
body: Clear owners without safety: owners hide problems until the deadline. Safety without owners: everyone shares problems and nobody acts on them. Remote teams need both.
Go easy on tracking, too. A few written habits help. Daily forms, online-status checks and cameras-on rules feel like surveillance, which quietly undoes the safety you built.

cards.title: The owner says she'll miss the date.
body: A week later, the developer posts in the team thread: her feature will be two days late. She's flagging it four days before the deadline.

options.text: Thank her publicly for the early warning, then ask her to post a new date and what she needs
options.feedback: Both concepts at once. The thanks protects **psychological safety**, and keeping her as owner with a new date keeps **accountability** clear.

options.text: Reply "No problem, take whatever time you need"
options.feedback: Kind, and it feels safe. But without a new date, ownership blurs and the team can't plan around her.

options.text: Quietly move the feature to a faster developer
options.feedback: The date might hold, but the team learns that flagging early gets your work taken away. Next time, they'll wait.

cards.title: Remote teams need safety and ownership, built in writing.
body: **Used here:** psychological safety, so "I'm stuck" is cheap to say, and roles and accountability, so every piece of work has one written owner.
**Try it today:** find one shared task in your team's chat with no clear owner. Name one person, a due date and the one place updates will go.
